item.title: Borrowing Horizons
item.description:
My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.

“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”

Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.

What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.

item.title: From Coding Agents to Loop Engineering: Building Engineering Memory for AI
item.description: Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow becomes more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but fundamentally it is still a pipeline.

item.title: Lowering the Cost of Curiosity
item.description:
I have been doing a lot of experimentation with local models recently, as have many of my colleagues. There is also a growing anticipation around the next generation of developer workstations and AI-focused boxes: machines capable of running increasingly useful models without sending every request to a SaaS platform.

It is easy to see this as another technology choice: local versus cloud, open model versus proprietary model, workstation versus API. I think the more interesting question for enterprises is economic.

item.title: Human in the loop isn’t the same as human judgement
item.description:
“Human in the loop” has become one of the standard answers to concerns about AI. We do not entirely trust the model, so we put a person somewhere in the process to validate what it has done. On the surface that sounds sensible, and sometimes it absolutely is.

But I think it exposes a much older problem in the way we design controls.

I’ve spent a lot of time working with security and compliance teams, and more recently with OT security teams where getting controls wrong can affect physical assets and operations as well as systems and data. I’ve seen similar patterns in higher education and charities, where safeguarding, accountability and practicality have to coexist across both physical and digital boundaries.

item.title: When Trust Becomes the Constraint
item.description:
One of the more difficult problems I keep coming back to with AI-assisted software modernisation isn’t really a technology problem. It’s trust.

We have all seen an LLM confidently make something up, merge two facts that happened to look similar, or produce an explanation that sounds entirely reasonable until someone who really understands the domain reads it. Once you have seen that happen a few times, it changes how you approach the capability, and that matters when we start asking AI to help modernise software.
